19179316.title: Weight loss to treat urinary incontinence in overweight and obese women
quotes: We randomly assigned 338 overweight and obese women with at least 10 urinary-incontinence episodes per week to an intensive 6-month weight-loss program that included diet, exercise, and behavior modification (226 patients) or to a structured education program (112 patients).
The women in the intervention group had a mean weight loss of 8.0% (7.8 kg), as compared with 1.6% (1.5 kg) in the control group (P<0.001).
After 6 months, the mean weekly number of incontinence episodes decreased by 47% in the intervention group, as compared with 28% in the control group (P=0.01).
As compared with the control group, the intervention group had a greater decrease in the frequency of stress-incontinence episodes (P=0.02), but not of urge-incontinence episodes (P=0.14).

analysis.note: Jabbit analysis. No study we found links GLP-1 drugs to pelvic organ prolapse; our PubMed search returned no records. Randomized weight-loss trials without drugs (PRIDE, Look AHEAD) found less urinary incontinence and no improvement or worsening in prolapse symptoms. 'Ozempic vulva' describes fat loss in the labia majora and mons, a weight-loss effect described by surgeons and clinicians; one large health-record abstract found no rise in coded vulvar atrophy or hypertrophy, but coded diagnoses miss cosmetic changes. Sexual side effects rest on case reports and reviews.
